content: Ragwort, scientifically known as Senecio jacobaea, is a member of the Asteraceae family and is a common wildflower found throughout Europe, particularly in dry, open areas. It has also spread as a weed to other parts of the world. In North America, a related species is Packera obovata. Ragwort is known by various names, including Cushag (Isle of Man), Buachalán Buí (Ireland), Tansy Ragwort, St. James-wort, Ragweed, Stinking Nanny, Staggerwort, Dog Standard, Cankerwort, Stammerwort, and Mare's Fart. In the western United States, it is often referred to as Tansy Ragwort or simply Tansy, though this is misleading as it bears only a superficial resemblance to true tansy, which has culinary uses. The plant is either biennial or perennial, with erect, straight stems that are sparsely hairy or hairless, reaching heights of 0.3 to 2.0 meters. Its leaves are pinnately lobed, with blunt terminal lobes, and emit an unpleasant odor, which explains the inclusion of stinking in many of its names.5 to 2.5 cm in diameter. They grow in dense, flat-topped clusters and bloom from June to November. Pollination is carried out by various bees, flies, moths, and butterflies. A single plant can produce 2,000 to 2,500 flowers in clusters of 20 to 60 heads, yielding between 75,000 and 200,000 seeds. However, in its native Eurasian range, most seeds fail to germinate or travel far from the parent plant. Two subspecies of Ragwort are recognized: 1. Senecio jacobaea ssp. jacobaea – the typical form with ray florets. 2. Senecio jacobaea ssp. dunensis – a form lacking ray florets. Ragwort thrives along roadsides, in waste grounds, and in regions with cool climates and high rainfall. It is native to Eurasia, spanning from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. In Britain and Ireland, it is classified as a weed. In the United States, it has been introduced and is primarily found in the Northwest and Northeast, including states such as California, Oregon, Washington, and New York. It is also present in Argentina, northern Africa, India, Siberia, New Zealand, and Australia. In many Australian states and in New Zealand, Ragwort is legally classified as a noxious weed, requiring landowners to eradicate it. Ragwort serves as a food source for the larvae of several moth species, including Cochylis atricapitana, Phycitodes maritima, and Phycitodes saxicolais. It is most notably associated with the Cinnabar moth (Tyria jacobaeae), whose caterpillars absorb the plant's toxic alkaloids, making them unpalatable to predators. The adult moths, which are red and black, are similarly distasteful. The Cinnabar moth has been introduced as a biological control agent in regions where Ragwort is invasive, such as New Zealand and the western United States. In New Zealand, the Ragwort flea beetle (Longitarsus jacobaea) has also been introduced for this purpose. Ragwort contains numerous alkaloids, particularly pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which are toxic to animals and humans. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified these alkaloids as harmful, with compounds such as jacobine, jaconine, jacozine, retrorsine, seneciphylline, senecionine, and senkirkine confirmed in the plant. Other alkaloids, such as riddelline and spartioidine, have also been reported. Ragwort poses a significant risk to livestock, particularly horses and cattle. While horses typically avoid the plant due to its bitter taste, ingestion of sufficient quantities can lead to irreversible liver damage, manifesting as cirrhosis. Symptoms of poisoning in horses include yellowing of the mucous membranes, depression, and lack of coordination. Sheep, on the other hand, can consume small amounts of Ragwort without immediate harm and may even benefit from its anthelmintic properties, as the alkaloids can kill intestinal worms. However, the toxic effects on the liver are cumulative, and repeated ingestion, even in small doses, can be fatal. There is no known antidote for Ragwort poisoning, though cessation of consumption may allow for recovery in some cases. Honey produced from Ragwort flowers has been found to contain trace amounts of alkaloids such as jacoline, jacobine, jacozine, senecionine, and seneciphylline. The WHO has also warned that humans consuming herbal remedies containing pyrrolizidine alkaloids may develop jaundice and face a high risk of death within 18 to 24 months. In the Republic of Ireland, Ragwort is classified as a noxious weed under the Noxious Weeds Act of 1936, requiring landowners to control its growth. In the United Kingdom, it is listed as an injurious weed under the Weeds Act of 1959, which allows authorities to mandate its control but does not make its growth illegal. The Ragwort Control Act of 2003 introduced a code of practice for managing the plant but did not impose additional legal obligations on landowners. Historically, Ragwort was used in traditional medicine for conditions such as eye inflammation, ulcers, rheumatism, sciatica, and gout. It was also applied externally for bee stings. Due to its alkaloid content, some researchers have explored its potential for inhibiting cancer cell growth. In ancient Greece and Rome, it was believed to have aphrodisiac properties. The plant's flowers and leaves have been used to produce dyes in shades of green, yellow, brown, and orange. Ragwort has also been referenced in literature and poetry. The Greek physician Dioscorides recommended it, as did early herbalists Gerard and Culpeper. The poet John Clare and Manx poet Josephine Kermode wrote positively about the plant, the latter referring to it as Cushag in her poem celebrating the Isle of Man. Ragwort is not cultivated, and no known varieties exist. Despite its reputation, it is often mistakenly referred to as the national flower of the Isle of Man, where the true national flower is Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris), known locally as Bollan Bane.
